frictionVectors.title: EU Gas Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Europe remains a critical market for Algerian gas, creating interdependence but also pressure over pricing, supply volumes, and political alignment.

frictionVectors.title: Sahel Security Spillover
frictionVectors.details: Instability across Mali, Niger, and Libya tests Algeria's border security while complicating its non-interventionist regional posture.

frictionVectors.title: Strategic Corridor Competition
frictionVectors.details: The Lobito Corridor attracts US, European, and Chinese interest because of its route to critical minerals, increasing Angola's leverage but also external pressure over infrastructure access.

frictionVectors.title: Debt-Linked Resource Exposure
frictionVectors.details: Chinese financing and longstanding oil-backed obligations continue to constrain policy flexibility despite efforts to diversify partnerships and production.

frictionVectors.title: Niger Border Trade Disruption
frictionVectors.details: Political tensions with Niger have disrupted established trade routes and exposed Benin's dependence on regional transit relationships and port access.

frictionVectors.title: Sahel Militancy Pressure
frictionVectors.details: Jihadist violence is moving southward toward northern Benin, threatening transport corridors, protected areas, and the state's control over frontier resources.

frictionVectors.title: Diamond Partnership Renegotiation
frictionVectors.details: Botswana's push for greater value capture and domestic beneficiation increases sovereign control but creates friction with established international mining partners.

frictionVectors.title: Critical Minerals Competition
frictionVectors.details: Foreign interest in copper, nickel, and other minerals offers diversification capital while raising concerns over concessions, processing capacity, and long-term value retention.

frictionVectors.title: Gold Sector Reassertion
frictionVectors.details: The government is seeking tighter control over gold production and marketing, challenging foreign operators and informal networks while risking lower output and investment.

frictionVectors.title: Russian Security Alignment
frictionVectors.details: Expanded security cooperation with Russia may strengthen regime autonomy from Western partners, but opaque arrangements and battlefield dependence create new external leverage.

frictionVectors.title: Nickel and mining concessions
frictionVectors.details: Burundi is seeking to convert major nickel potential into state revenue, but foreign capital, limited processing capacity, and opaque concession terms constrain domestic control.

frictionVectors.title: Transport and energy bottlenecks
frictionVectors.details: Dependence on Tanzanian and other regional corridors, alongside chronic electricity shortages, limits Burundi's ability to capture value from its resources.

frictionVectors.title: Port and maritime infrastructure dependence
frictionVectors.details: Foreign-backed port, airport, and logistics investment strengthens Cabo Verde's connectivity but leaves critical infrastructure exposed to external commercial and strategic priorities.

frictionVectors.title: Water and energy import exposure
frictionVectors.details: The archipelago remains dependent on imported fuel, desalination systems, and external financing, limiting resilience despite progress in renewable energy and fisheries governance.

highlights: Oil and gas leverage remains limited

frictionVectors.title: Hydrocarbon and mining concessions
frictionVectors.details: Foreign firms retain significant influence across oil, gas, and mineral value chains, while limited refining and processing capacity reduces Cameroon's domestic capture of resource rents.

frictionVectors.title: Logistics corridors and external finance
frictionVectors.details: Chinese-backed infrastructure and Gulf-linked commercial interests compete with Western and regional partners around ports, roads, and rail, increasing strategic dependence without resolving governance weaknesses.

frictionVectors.title: Gold and diamond concessions
frictionVectors.details: Foreign-linked mining networks and armed intermediaries continue to capture value from gold and diamonds, while weak regulation limits state oversight and local benefit.

frictionVectors.title: Russian security and resource ties
frictionVectors.details: The government's reliance on Russian security support has increased regime autonomy from some Western actors but risks substituting one externally dependent security-resource relationship for another.

frictionVectors.title: Oil-sector external dependence
frictionVectors.details: International operators and external buyers remain central to production, transport, and marketing, leaving Chad vulnerable to price shocks and limiting transparent domestic control of revenues.

frictionVectors.title: Security corridors and border pressure
frictionVectors.details: Instability around Libya, Sudan, and the Central African Republic places transport and energy infrastructure at risk while sustaining dependence on foreign security partnerships.

frictionVectors.title: Mayotte and maritime sovereignty
frictionVectors.details: France retains control of Mayotte, sustaining a major sovereignty dispute and limiting Comoros' effective control over surrounding maritime resources.

frictionVectors.title: External dependence and port access
frictionVectors.details: Comoros relies heavily on foreign budget support, remittances, and infrastructure finance, leaving strategic transport and energy decisions vulnerable to outside leverage.

frictionVectors.title: Mineral supply-chain competition
frictionVectors.details: Copper, cobalt, and other strategic minerals attract competing Chinese, Western, and regional interests, while weak oversight limits the state's share of value and revenue.

frictionVectors.title: M23 and regional security
frictionVectors.details: Armed conflict in the east, including M23 activity and tensions involving Rwanda, continues to undermine territorial control, mining governance, and infrastructure security.

frictionVectors.title: Hydrocarbon dependence
frictionVectors.details: Oil dominates export earnings and public finance, exposing sovereignty and development planning to production shocks, opaque contracting, and external energy firms.

frictionVectors.title: Debt-linked infrastructure exposure
frictionVectors.details: Chinese-financed roads, ports, and other projects improve connectivity but increase dependence on external contractors, lenders, and future resource revenues.

highlights: Abidjan emerges as a regional hub

frictionVectors.title: Cocoa sovereignty gap
frictionVectors.details: Côte d'Ivoire has strengthened domestic regulation and processing ambitions, but foreign traders, processors, and volatile global prices still capture substantial value.

frictionVectors.title: Regional security spillover
frictionVectors.details: Instability in the Sahel pressures northern border security and defense spending, while external security partnerships influence the country's strategic posture.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign military concentration
frictionVectors.details: U.S., Chinese, French, Japanese, and other foreign military facilities provide revenue and leverage but constrain Djibouti's strategic autonomy and expose it to great-power rivalry.

frictionVectors.title: Port and debt dependence
frictionVectors.details: The economy depends heavily on foreign-operated ports, logistics corridors, and external financing, particularly amid competition with Ethiopia-linked and Chinese-backed infrastructure.

frictionVectors.title: External Financing Dependence
frictionVectors.details: IMF programs and substantial Gulf investment provide essential liquidity but increase outside influence over state assets, currency policy, and strategic infrastructure.

frictionVectors.title: GERD and Nile Water Dispute
frictionVectors.details: Egypt continues to oppose Ethiopia's unilateral control of Nile flows, keeping regional water security and diplomatic escalation risks elevated.

frictionVectors.title: Hydrocarbon Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Falling oil and gas production constrains fiscal sovereignty while foreign energy firms retain major influence over extraction, liquefaction, and technical capacity.

frictionVectors.title: Debt-Linked Infrastructure
frictionVectors.details: Chinese-backed construction and financing remain important to the government's development model, creating long-term exposure to external creditors and contractors.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign Mining Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Gold and base-metal revenues depend heavily on foreign operators and opaque joint ventures, limiting domestic control over strategic mineral value chains.

frictionVectors.title: Red Sea Militarization
frictionVectors.details: Eritrea's coastline has heightened strategic value amid regional conflict, increasing competition among Gulf, Middle Eastern, and other external actors for access and influence.

frictionVectors.title: South African Economic Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Customs revenues, trade routes, electricity links, and investment remain closely tied to South Africa, limiting Eswatini's room for independent economic policy.

frictionVectors.title: Political Reform Pressure
frictionVectors.details: External donors and civil-society networks continue pressing for political opening, while the monarchy seeks to preserve control over land, security, and strategic assets.

frictionVectors.title: Nile Basin Confrontation
frictionVectors.details: The Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam strengthens Ethiopia's control over its water infrastructure but continues to generate acute tensions with Egypt and Sudan.

frictionVectors.title: External Financing and Port Access
frictionVectors.details: Debt restructuring and the search for dependable port access expose Addis Ababa to leverage from international creditors and neighboring coastal states.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign control of strategic minerals
frictionVectors.details: The government is seeking greater national participation in oil and manganese while retaining foreign capital and technical operators. Renegotiation risks could unsettle established French, Chinese, and other commercial interests.

frictionVectors.title: Transport and fiscal dependence
frictionVectors.details: Rail, port, and energy infrastructure remain crucial bottlenecks for sovereign resource monetization. Fiscal pressure limits Libreville's ability to finance these systems without external lenders or investors.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign pressure on fisheries
frictionVectors.details: Industrial fishing agreements and weak monitoring constrain Gambian control over marine resources. Local communities continue to challenge opaque licensing and limited domestic value capture.

frictionVectors.title: Port and energy dependence
frictionVectors.details: The country's trade and electricity systems depend heavily on external finance and regional connectivity through Senegal. This creates leverage for donors, neighboring states, and foreign operators over strategic infrastructure.

frictionVectors.title: Illegal mining and environmental loss
frictionVectors.details: Artisanal and illegal gold mining continues to damage waterways, farmland, and state legitimacy. Efforts to formalize production and increase public capture face entrenched local networks and foreign-linked trading channels.

frictionVectors.title: Critical-minerals bargaining
frictionVectors.details: Ghana is seeking stronger domestic processing and public returns from gold, lithium, and other minerals while managing IMF-linked fiscal constraints. External investors retain significant leverage over technology, financing, and export access.

frictionVectors.title: Simandou foreign consortium control
frictionVectors.details: The Simandou iron-ore corridor offers major state revenue potential but depends on foreign mining consortia, railways, and port infrastructure. Concession terms and local-content enforcement will determine whether the project strengthens or dilutes Guinean sovereignty.

frictionVectors.title: Political transition and resource opacity
frictionVectors.details: Military-led rule and uncertainty over the political timetable weaken oversight of mining contracts and public revenue. International partners can exploit the governance gap while the state prioritizes rapid project delivery.

frictionVectors.title: Cashew value-chain capture
frictionVectors.details: The economy remains heavily dependent on raw cashew exports, leaving farmers and the state vulnerable to foreign traders, price volatility, and limited domestic processing. Weak institutions reduce bargaining power over contracts and standards.

frictionVectors.title: Illicit maritime networks
frictionVectors.details: Drug-trafficking routes and weak coastal enforcement undermine state control of maritime territory. Offshore resource prospects and fisheries also invite external actors into an environment where regulatory capacity remains limited.

frictionVectors.title: External debt and infrastructure leverage
frictionVectors.details: Chinese and other external infrastructure financing continues to shape Nairobi's fiscal and strategic choices. Debt-service pressure limits the state's room to renegotiate major transport and energy projects.

frictionVectors.title: Port and corridor competition
frictionVectors.details: Kenya's control of Mombasa and the Lamu corridor is challenged by regional competition, insecurity, and foreign-backed logistics alternatives. These pressures affect Kenya's ability to convert transport infrastructure into sovereign influence.

highlights: Water exports deepen dependence on Pretoria

frictionVectors.title: Water sovereignty versus South African demand
frictionVectors.details: The Lesotho Highlands Water Project provides vital revenue but ties national resource security to South Africa's financing, infrastructure, and consumption needs. Delays, cost overruns, or disputes could reduce Lesotho's bargaining power.

frictionVectors.title: Transport and energy vulnerability
frictionVectors.details: Lesotho remains structurally dependent on South African corridors and imported energy. This limits strategic autonomy and exposes the country to external policy shifts and infrastructure bottlenecks.

highlights: Port access remains a sovereignty test

frictionVectors.title: Foreign control of mineral value chains
frictionVectors.details: Iron ore and gold production rely heavily on foreign capital, operators, and export infrastructure. Liberia captures royalties and employment, but limited domestic processing leaves substantial value outside the country.

frictionVectors.title: Concession and port governance
frictionVectors.details: Long-term concessions and dependence on major port operators constrain the state's ability to revise commercial terms. Contract transparency and local-content enforcement remain central sovereignty concerns.

highlights: Oil wealth remains divided by rival authorities

frictionVectors.title: Fragmented control of oil infrastructure
frictionVectors.details: Competing political and armed networks continue to influence fields, terminals, and export decisions. Disruptions or blockades can rapidly convert resource control into fiscal and security crises.

frictionVectors.title: External military and commercial leverage
frictionVectors.details: Foreign states and private actors retain influence through security partnerships, arms relationships, and energy interests. This weakens unified national authority over strategic infrastructure and contract policy.

highlights: Energy and transport gaps weaken bargaining power

frictionVectors.title: Mining concessions and value capture
frictionVectors.details: Nickel, cobalt, graphite, ilmenite, and other mineral projects depend substantially on foreign capital and overseas processing networks. Madagascar faces persistent pressure to expand production faster than it can strengthen fiscal, environmental, and local-benefit controls.

frictionVectors.title: Infrastructure dependence
frictionVectors.details: Weak roads, ports, and electricity systems increase reliance on project-linked foreign infrastructure and financing. This can improve production capacity while narrowing the government's room to set independent terms.

frictionVectors.title: Mining Deals and Fiscal Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Malawi is seeking foreign capital for uranium, rare earths and other mineral projects while restructuring external debt. Weak bargaining leverage and limited processing capacity risk leaving the country dependent on low-value extraction and imported technology.

frictionVectors.title: Fuel and Electricity Vulnerability
frictionVectors.details: Foreign-exchange shortages and reliance on imported fuel constrain sovereign control over transport and power infrastructure. Regional grid and corridor disruptions can quickly transmit into domestic shortages.

highlights: Gold Sovereignty Drive Confronts Production Declines

frictionVectors.title: Junta Pressure on Foreign Miners
frictionVectors.details: Authorities are seeking a larger state share of gold revenues and tighter control over industrial mining. Contract renegotiations and regulatory uncertainty may increase fiscal receipts but also deter investment and technical capacity.

frictionVectors.title: Security Dependence on Russia
frictionVectors.details: The military government has reduced reliance on Western security partners while deepening cooperation with Russian-linked forces. This limits diplomatic flexibility and can expose mining corridors and infrastructure to greater insecurity.

highlights: Gas Export Era Begins Under External Operators
Iron Ore Logistics Remain Strategic Chokepoints

frictionVectors.title: Greater Tortue Ahmeyim Revenue Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Offshore gas exports with Senegal are operated through foreign-led consortia, giving Mauritania revenue and infrastructure opportunities but limiting immediate domestic control over technology and marketing. Production timing and cost overruns remain important sovereignty risks.

frictionVectors.title: SNIM and Atlantic Corridor Exposure
frictionVectors.details: Iron ore earnings depend heavily on SNIM, rail capacity and the Nouadhibou export route. Foreign equipment, financing and logistics expertise remain difficult to replace, while Sahel instability raises protection costs.

highlights: Indian Ocean Position Attracts Competing Partners

frictionVectors.title: Chagos Sovereignty and Security Transition
frictionVectors.details: The long-running transfer process concerning the Chagos Archipelago and the Diego Garcia base remains central to Mauritian sovereignty. Any settlement must balance territorial claims, security arrangements and the interests of the United Kingdom and United States.

frictionVectors.title: External Capital in Ports and Digital Infrastructure
frictionVectors.details: Indian, Chinese, European and Gulf-linked investment is expanding competition around ports, connectivity and finance. Mauritius retains strong regulatory capacity, but strategic infrastructure requires careful screening to avoid asymmetric dependence.

frictionVectors.title: Western Sahara Resource Diplomacy
frictionVectors.details: Phosphate, fisheries, renewable-energy and infrastructure projects in Western Sahara remain tied to Morocco's sovereignty strategy. Disputes with the Polisario Front and legal challenges in European markets create continuing political and commercial exposure.

frictionVectors.title: External Technology and Energy Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Morocco is building domestic value chains in fertilizers, electric vehicles and renewables, but still relies on foreign technology, finance and imported energy inputs. European market access and Chinese industrial participation create both leverage and dependency risks.

highlights: LNG ambitions constrained by Cabo Delgado insecurity
Rwanda-backed security stabilizes strategic gas zone

frictionVectors.title: Cabo Delgado LNG Corridor
frictionVectors.details: Insurgency continues to limit Mozambique's control over the gas-producing north and delays major foreign-led LNG projects. Kigali's security role improves protection but underscores Maputo's dependence on external forces.

frictionVectors.title: Resource Revenue Bargaining
frictionVectors.details: The government is seeking greater fiscal and local-content benefits from multinational gas developers while remaining dependent on foreign capital, technology, and security support.

frictionVectors.title: Offshore Oil and Gas Control
frictionVectors.details: Recent offshore discoveries have increased Namibia's leverage but also its exposure to major international energy firms. Negotiations over fiscal terms, local participation, and environmental safeguards will determine how much value remains domestically.

frictionVectors.title: Green Hydrogen Infrastructure
frictionVectors.details: Foreign-backed hydrogen and port projects could diversify the economy, but financing, water access, and export infrastructure may leave Namibia dependent on external sponsors unless domestic ownership expands.

highlights: Security and sanctions constrain economic autonomy

frictionVectors.title: Uranium and Mining Revisions
frictionVectors.details: Niamey is seeking greater control and revenue from uranium and other extractive assets while reducing French influence. Contract disputes and operational uncertainty risk lowering investment and export capacity.

frictionVectors.title: Russian Security Dependence
frictionVectors.details: The withdrawal of Western forces and arrival of Russian-linked security support shift external influence rather than eliminate it. Persistent jihadist violence limits the state's ability to secure mining zones and transport corridors.

highlights: Oil theft and grid weakness erode state control

frictionVectors.title: Pipeline and Oil-Security Crisis
frictionVectors.details: The state is trying to recover production from theft, sabotage, and illegal refining while attracting international operators. Weak enforcement and opaque contracting continue to reduce public capture of petroleum value.

frictionVectors.title: Refinery and Gas Infrastructure
frictionVectors.details: Domestic refining and gas projects can reduce import dependence, but financing, technical partnerships, and unreliable electricity infrastructure keep Nigeria reliant on external capital and expertise.

highlights: State capacity remains strong and centralized
Eastern Congo links security to mineral access

frictionVectors.title: Great Lakes Mineral Trade
frictionVectors.details: Rwanda's security posture and alleged links to mineral flows from eastern Democratic Republic of the Congo generate sustained international scrutiny. Kigali rejects accusations of predatory extraction, but the dispute directly affects its sovereignty narrative and external relations.

frictionVectors.title: External Security and Infrastructure Finance
frictionVectors.details: Rwanda retains strong domestic control while relying on foreign aid, investment, and security partnerships for development. Conditions attached to that support can narrow policy space despite effective state administration.

frictionVectors.title: Gulf of Guinea Offshore Exploration
frictionVectors.details: Exploration interest remains constrained by uncertain commercial prospects and limited domestic technical capacity. Foreign operators and licensing terms could shape the country's future petroleum leverage.

frictionVectors.title: External Infrastructure Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Port, energy, and connectivity projects rely heavily on external finance and contractors, leaving São Tomé exposed to debt, repayment, and strategic-access pressures.

frictionVectors.title: Oil and Gas Contract Renegotiation
frictionVectors.details: The government is seeking greater national participation and fiscal returns from new offshore production while managing inherited contracts, investor confidence, and debt constraints.

frictionVectors.title: Fishing Access and Coastal Control
frictionVectors.details: Foreign fishing access and declining coastal stocks remain politically sensitive. Enforcement capacity and opaque licensing can undermine local livelihoods and maritime sovereignty.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign Fishing Pressure
frictionVectors.details: Seychelles retains strong regulatory institutions but remains dependent on foreign vessels, markets, and monitoring support. Tuna access and illegal fishing continue to test control over its maritime zone.

frictionVectors.title: Infrastructure and Security Competition
frictionVectors.details: Port, surveillance, and connectivity partnerships involve India, France, China, and other external actors. The government generally preserves strategic autonomy by balancing these relationships.

frictionVectors.title: Iron Ore and Critical Minerals Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Mining revenues and export logistics remain dominated by foreign capital and commodity cycles. Government efforts to secure better terms and local processing face financing and infrastructure constraints.

frictionVectors.title: Energy and Transport Bottlenecks
frictionVectors.details: Unreliable electricity, limited rail capacity, and weak port-to-mine links raise costs and strengthen the bargaining position of external operators and infrastructure financiers.

frictionVectors.title: Offshore Oil and Licensing Disputes
frictionVectors.details: Prospective offshore resources attract foreign operators and competing political authorities, while unresolved federal-regional jurisdiction and revenue-sharing rules limit sovereign control.

frictionVectors.title: Security and Port Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Turkey, Gulf states, Western partners, and other actors provide security and port-related support, but their involvement can create overlapping strategic commitments and constrain independent policy.

frictionVectors.title: Rail, Port, and Power Bottlenecks
frictionVectors.details: Chronic constraints at Transnet railways and ports continue to reduce export sovereignty, especially for minerals. Grid reliability is improving but remains vulnerable to aging infrastructure and financing gaps.

frictionVectors.title: Competing External Mineral Agendas
frictionVectors.details: Chinese, Western, and Gulf actors are competing for access to platinum-group metals, manganese, and other strategic minerals. Pretoria is attempting to preserve beneficiation and policy autonomy while attracting investment.

frictionVectors.title: Sudan Pipeline Vulnerability
frictionVectors.details: South Sudan remains dependent on export infrastructure crossing war-torn Sudan, leaving oil revenues exposed to pipeline damage, political leverage, and transit uncertainty.

frictionVectors.title: Oil-Financed Patronage Networks
frictionVectors.details: Opaque production-sharing, advances, and security-linked arrangements limit public control over petroleum revenue. Regional actors and foreign oil firms retain substantial leverage over the sector.

frictionVectors.title: Gold Smuggling and Foreign Sponsorship
frictionVectors.details: Gold production and trading networks are increasingly tied to armed factions and external patrons, weakening state control and diverting revenue from national institutions.

frictionVectors.title: Port Sudan Strategic Competition
frictionVectors.details: The Red Sea coast and Port Sudan are exposed to competing Gulf, Russian, Egyptian, and other security and commercial interests. The war has made logistics infrastructure a bargaining asset for rival authorities.

highlights: Ports and Corridors Gain Strategic Weight

frictionVectors.title: Foreign-Controlled Port Infrastructure
frictionVectors.details: Port concessions and logistics partnerships, including Gulf-linked investment, could improve trade capacity while creating long-term concerns over tariff authority and strategic control.

frictionVectors.title: Delayed LNG Development
frictionVectors.details: Large gas projects remain important to Tanzania's fiscal and energy ambitions but face negotiation, financing, and local-content pressures. Foreign operators retain substantial influence over capital-intensive development.

highlights: Phosphate and Transit Revenues Remain Concentrated

frictionVectors.title: Port and Corridor Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Lomé's importance as a Gulf of Guinea transshipment and Sahel supply hub gives foreign shipping and logistics firms significant leverage over national trade infrastructure.

frictionVectors.title: Sahel Spillover and Security Partnerships
frictionVectors.details: Instability around Burkina Faso and northern Togo is increasing security costs and inviting deeper external military and intelligence involvement. This may constrain sovereign control over border infrastructure and trade routes.

frictionVectors.title: EU migration and financing dependence
frictionVectors.details: European funding and market access remain tied to migration control, limiting Tunisia's policy autonomy. Fiscal stress and stalled external financing increase outside leverage.

frictionVectors.title: Energy import vulnerability
frictionVectors.details: Tunisia remains heavily dependent on imported hydrocarbons and electricity support from Algeria. Renewable projects offer diversification but rely substantially on foreign capital and technology.

frictionVectors.title: EACOP financing and sanctions pressure
frictionVectors.details: The Lake Albert oil project is strengthening Uganda's prospective export position but remains exposed to Western sanctions, financing constraints, and environmental litigation. China and other non-Western partners are helping offset that pressure.

frictionVectors.title: Transport dependence through neighbors
frictionVectors.details: Uganda's trade and future oil exports depend on corridors through Kenya and Tanzania. Border disruptions, regional insecurity, or diplomatic disputes could raise costs and constrain sovereign control.

highlights: Debt restructuring restores room to maneuver

frictionVectors.title: Foreign competition for copper assets
frictionVectors.details: Zambia is using renewed copper demand to attract investment from Chinese, Gulf, US, and European actors. Competition improves bargaining power but risks leaving technology, processing, and revenue control externally concentrated.

frictionVectors.title: Power shortages constrain mining sovereignty
frictionVectors.details: Hydropower shortfalls and climate variability have disrupted mining output and increased dependence on regional electricity imports. Energy insecurity weakens Zambia's ability to capture value from copper expansion.

frictionVectors.title: Lithium and mineral ownership pressure
frictionVectors.details: Zimbabwe is pushing local processing and restricting exports of some unprocessed minerals, but Chinese capital and external technology remain central to lithium and other mining projects. The state has increased policy leverage without yet securing broad domestic value capture.

frictionVectors.title: Gold and sanctions-related financial channels
frictionVectors.details: Gold remains a crucial source of foreign exchange but is vulnerable to smuggling, opaque trading networks, and sanctions-related restrictions. These channels reduce transparency and weaken public control over mineral revenues.
